As the birthplace of so many of our nation's democratic institutions, Virginia is a natural place to begin America's 250th anniversary. but just as important as where we begin is how we begin. We in Virginia are centering this historic commemoration on the story of our tribal nations and their inherent sovereignty.

That choice reflects a simple but powerful truth that civic renewal begins with telling the full and truthful story of our nation's founding. Long before 1776, tribal nations governed themselves on this continent. They developed sophisticated systems of diplomacy, law, representation, consensus building.

They entered into treaties. They defended their lands. They exercised sovereignty, not as a gift from any other government, but as an inherent right in that sovereignty endures today. Tribal nations are sovereign governments with enduring rights and treaty relationships with the United States.

Recognizing that reality is not an act of charity. It's an act of constitutional fidelity and historical honesty. We acknowledge that indigenous governance helped shape the democratic ideas that became foundational to the United States.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also known as the Iroquois Confederacy, offers a model of federalism, representative leadership, and balance of powers that influence early American thinkers. As we celebrate 250 years of American democracy, it is fitting that we honor those intellectual and political contributions.
